questions.question: should I treat my boots out of box ? Annnnd how often should I treat them ?

hybrid.answer:
It depends on the boot. For pretreated leather, no. For distressed or rustic leather, yes. As for how often, I treat mine when they look or feel like they need it, not on a fixed schedule.

**Out of the box**
- From what I found, Blundstone says most of their boots come pretreated and doesn't recommend treating them out of the box [1]. That's the brand's guidance, not mine.
- The exception is rustic brown, Crazy Horse brown and rustic black leathers. Those are distressed and don't carry the same pretreatment as finished, oiled leather [2].
- For rustic boots like mine, I highly recommend conditioning them rather than leaving them dry. They'll look different (darker), but they'll last longer [3].
- I haven't covered other brands or leathers beyond that, so I can't say whether yours come pretreated.

**How often**
- I don't follow a strict schedule. I do it when I feel they need it, and I know plenty of people are more regimented [4].
- How often depends on how much you wear them, what you do in them and where you go [4].
- Signs they need more care:
  - If they look or feel dry, or they've stopped beading water on top, they probably need more wax [4].
  - If they look dry, they need oil [4].
  - If they're dirty, clean them. Dirt wears the leather down faster [4].
- Any leather you haven't conditioned in a few months is worth conditioning [3].
- Early on, I said you might need to wax them every month, or even every week if you're really hard on them [5]. My later view is looser and based on how the boots look and feel.

**Order of steps:** clean, then condition, then wax [6].

questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, they get tighter the first time you get them wet, mostly in the waist. They then loosen again as you wear them.

**How much they shrink**
- Shrink-to-fit 501s shrink noticeably after a soak. When I did it, they slimmed up mainly in the waist [1], and the length barely changed [2].
- Mine were very snug at first. A week later the waist and thighs had stretched enough to wear a belt [3].
- Wearing them often brings them back to about the size of a regular rinsed pair [4].

**Sizing**
- I go two sizes up in the waist [5]. Levi's advice is also two inches more in length [6].
- I didn't follow that at first. I bought a 29 waist and could barely pull them on [7]. After trying this a few times I now say Levi's advice is correct [6].
- For you, that means buying two waist sizes above your usual and two extra inches of length.

**Washing**
- To avoid shrinking them tighter than needed, don't use very hot water and don't put them in the dryer [8].

questions.question: I'm usually a 33x30 in Levi's 502s, what size should I buy in these? [501 STF]

hybrid.answer:
Go two sizes up in the waist and two inches longer than usual. For you that's a **35x32**.

**The rule I use:** My most recent advice on the 501 STF is to size up two sizes [1]. Levi's recommends going two sizes bigger in the waist and two inches longer than you'd normally wear, and after several pairs I agree they're right [2]. The waist number on an STF doesn't match the finished size, so you size up two because it shrinks down [3].

**Waist:** Your 33 becomes a 35. I don't know whether a 35 is offered. I did note that for a 34, a 36 might not exist.

**Length:** Your 30 becomes a 32. I wore a 30 length myself and wish I'd bought a 32 [4].

**Why I changed my mind:** At first I ignored Levi's sizing advice because jeans are usually too long on me [5]. I bought a 29 waist and could barely pull them on [4]. It worked out, because after wear they fit well [4]. Later I concluded that Levi's advice is correct [2].

**Not covered:** I haven't compared how the 502 fits against the 501 STF, so I can't say whether your 502 size carries over beyond applying this rule.

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

hybrid.answer:
I cuff mainly because I can't settle on one hem length. I never know whether I want no break, half break or full break, and cuffing is the only fix I've found short of committing to one fit [1].

- **Style:** My current style doesn't suit wider-legged pants worn uncuffed, so I cuffed my Levi's 501s [2]. I'd also have bought them in a 32 length, so the cuff partly makes up for the length I got wrong [2].
- **Length:** If jeans look too long, they just look bad to me, and a cuff fixes that. The 501s fit a little better with a basic cuff than uncut [3].
- **Boots:** I used to always cuff, but with boots I now like jeans worn over them a bit more [4].

Cuffing does make your legs look shorter [5], and a viewer once told me to uncuff my pants [1]. A cuff is a workaround for me, not a goal.

questions.question: So do you prefer [the Red Wing 3335s] over the 1907s?

hybrid.answer:
Mostly yes, but I've hedged lately. I used to say the 3335s were my favorite Red Wings, and I've since said they still might be, but probably not [1]. I'm also selling them [2].

**Why I liked the 3335s more**
- I called them my favorite boots I've ever had, ahead of the 1907s and the 875s [3].
- I'm not doing heritage work, I'm hiking and walking in the woods, and for that they're a dramatically better all-around boot [3].
- They're stitch-down and lighter, so they feel more nimble and are easier to walk in [4].

**Where the 1907s still win**
- The 1907s and 875s are more beefily constructed, so if you need a tough boot, the 3335s are probably not the ones to go for [5].
- If you're looking at a moc toe Red Wing, I think you should get the 1907s [6]. I also highly recommend them [7].

**Where I've landed**
The 875s, the 1907s and the Iron Rangers each have characteristics I really like [1]. For light hiking and walking, the 3335s are what I reached for.

**Where I stand**
- The 585s have held up through constant wear and stayed probably my most water resistant boots [1].
- I still count slip-on shoes like Blundstones as ones I can put on quickly in any weather [2]. I'm keeping those, though I could easily put them on the sell list [2].

- Earlier, I said they're worth the hype, and they're still some of my favorites even though they aren't as repairable as Goodyear-welted boots like Red Wings or Wolverines [3].

**The heavy-duty Blundstones**
I also had the heavy-duty Blundstone work boots. I let those go [7].

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
**Short answer:** I'd go with Solovair over the Made in England Docs. Solovairs are about $40 cheaper and better built [1][2].

**Price and value:** The England Docs cost about a third more because of the Made in England part, and Solovair doesn't carry that markup [2][3]. Judged on value alone, the extra $90 for the England boots isn't worth it, so you'd have to be a mega fan to buy them [4][5].

**Leather:** The England Docs have better leather that should age fine, and I think it's probably on par with Solovair [6]. Solovair uses full grain leather on certain models, while Docs generally don't. Check the specific model before you buy [7].

**Midsole and comfort:** Both the England Docs and Solovair have felted midsoles, but Solovair's are thicker, heavier and more robust [8][9]. Solovairs also have a shank, which makes them more comfortable over long periods. Docs have none [10].

**Repairs:** Solovair makes its boots easier to resole, and you can order soles from its website to repair them yourself [11][12]. Docs are hard to resole, partly because the original soles aren't available [13].

**Where the England Docs win:** The yellow stitching. If it matters to you, you have to get the Made in England Docs [14].

**Solovair downsides:** I had a quality-control problem with my first Solovair monkey boots, a pull tab and a lace ripped. I think the laces may be vulnerable because of the rough eyelets, and that's my only gripe with Solovair [15]. Sizing was also off on my pair, which came out really big [16].

questions.question: Hi, I am going on a 4 day hike and I am wondering if I can use my blundstone for them, what do you think?

hybrid.answer:
I haven't covered multi-day hiking in Blundstones, so I can't give you a verdict on four days. Here is what I did find on shorter hikes.

- **Ankle support:** Blundstones are not good boots for mountaining, apparently because they lack good ankle support [1]. I still took mine up and down a few mountains in Maine, and they held up well, though they got a little scuffed [1]. If your route is rugged, that missing support is the main thing I'd think about.
- **Comfort and break-in:** When I first got them I walked around a city all day and through the woods with no blisters [2]. Later I got break-in blisters when I started running and walking the track in them, and those stopped after two to three weeks [3]. So I wouldn't take a pair on a long trip without wearing them in first.
- **Wet conditions:** Mine have stayed probably my most water resistant boots through years of wear [4]. They are water resistant, not waterproof. If you want that resistance, buy them knowing you'll have to take care of them and keep them treated [5].
- **Overall:** I think they're decent for work but not incredible [6]. I see them as a balanced everyday boot rather than a specialist one.

questions.question: I'm 5'11-225 lbs with a dad bod. What's the most cost efficient and quality t shirt for me? Also, what size would u prefer?

hybrid.answer:
For you at 5'11" and 225 lbs, I'd go with the Muji tee. If you want the cheapest good option, the Uniqlo tee is the budget pick.

**Muji (my pick for you)**
- Uniqlo at $20 is probably the best t-shirt you can get for the price [1]. But if you're taller or wider, I'd go with Muji instead [2].
- Muji costs about $4 or $5 more, but it's significantly longer and a good deal wider [2].
- In an earlier comparison I said Muji's extra cost feels justified, because the shirt feels better [3].

**Other value options**
- **House of Blanks:** $35, made in Canada, and it had no torque at all. I called it an outstanding value [4].
- **Bronson:** At $29 it's a very, very good shirt [5].
- **Los Angeles Apparel:** It runs very large and fits me a bit like a tent [6]. If you size down one, it might win [7].

**Size**
I haven't given a size recommendation for your measurements, so I can't name one. The closest guidance I have is about fit. For a shirt that sits well, I like a lot of space across the shoulders [8]. Muji is already cut longer and wider, so you may not need to size up [2]. Los Angeles Apparel runs large, so I'd size down one [7].

questions.question: Where's Whitesville?? It's literally the most well known White Tee from Japan

hybrid.answer:
Whitesville is in my t-shirt ranking, and I also covered their sweatshirt.

**Whitesville tee**
- I'd really recommend it [1]. It's by far one of the softest t-shirts on the list [1].
- It comes from a Japanese company riffing on old Americana underwear, so it's cut tight like vintage tees were [1].
- I wouldn't say it's worth the price until you look at the collar. It has binding tape over it, so it holds its shape better over time [1].
- In the shrink test it lost 5.4% in width and 3% in length [2].
- It won my award for the softest, coziest shirt [3].

**Whitesville sweatshirt**
- It's one of the best sweatshirts on that list. It's a fantastic-quality loopwheel sweatshirt from Japan, though I don't love its look [4].
- It uses a 5x1 rib knit on the cuffs, hem and collar. You either like that or you don't, and I'd prefer a 2x1 or 1x1 [4].
- It's very loose and soft, in a fluffy, cozy way rather than a silky one. It's the one to get if that's what you want [4][5].
- It's pre-washed, so shrinkage was zero [5].

I don't name one shirt for everyone, because the best t-shirt depends on your preferences [1]. If you want a short list, here's where I land.

**1. Uniqlo (about $20).** This is probably the best t-shirt you can get for the price [2]. It's the starter shirt [3]. If you're taller or wider, get Muji instead [3].

**2. Front General Store or House of Blanks (about $35-40).** Front General Store is the one I'm feeling right now, and tomorrow I might pick House of Blanks [4]. Choose Front General Store if you want character and feel. Choose House of Blanks if you want perfectly smooth with no torque [4]. House of Blanks showed zero torquing [5].

**3. Merz b. Schwanen 2M15 (if you're spending more).** In the nicer, cleaner category I gave it a slight edge over Lady White [6]. It's the updated version of the shirt from The Bear and is more universally pleasing [7].

If you'd rather have a mid-priced all-rounder, I'd go with the J. Press x American Trench [8]. Bronson also usually wins or comes close in t-shirt comparisons [9].

questions.question: 1907 vs the 875's? What's the difference?

hybrid.answer:
The 1907 and 875 are both Red Wing moc toes, and I'd go for the 1907. It costs about $10 more, and what you get for that money is a storm welt, a removable leather footbed and leather laces. [1][2]

**Price and what's included**
- The 1907 is about ten dollars more than the 875. [1]
- The 1907 comes with Red Wing's leather footbed, which you can typically buy separately for 40. [1]
- It also comes with leather laces, typically 15 on their own. [1]
- The footbed can be pulled out at the end of the day so the boots dry faster. [1]

**Construction**
- The 875 is Goodyear welted. I find that welt durable and pretty water resistant, and the space it creates is where the cork insole goes. [3]
- The 1907 has a storm welt, which to me is invaluable. [1]
- From what I've seen on Reddit, the popular view is that Red Wing's storm welt is just another strip of leather stitched onto the welt. I'm not quite sure that's all it is. [4]
- Both boots have crepe soles, which I expect to break down faster than the Vibram sole on the 3335. [5]

**Water resistance**
- In my standing-in-water test, one 1907 leaked almost immediately through the stitching and the other stayed dry. I'd still expect them to hold up fine in rain, grass or mud. [6]
- Leather welted boots in general aren't great for water resistance, so I mostly wear the 1907s day to day. [7]
- I haven't tested the 875 for water.

**Overall**
- If you're looking at a moc toe Red Wing, I think you should get the 1907. [8] I highly recommend them. [9]
- Both are more heavily built than the stitch-down 3335, which I like better as an all-around boot. [10]
- I like the characteristics of the 875, the 1907 and the Iron Ranger each in their own way. [11]

questions.question: How does Uniqlo compare to The Front General Store,  Proclub, and Hanes? ie what is the best budget shirt?

hybrid.answer:
**Short answer:** For price against quality, I'd go with Uniqlo. At $20 it's probably the best t-shirt you can get for the money [1]. If you want to spend a bit more for something with more character, I'd go with The Front General Store. I haven't ranked Pro Club or Hanes directly against Uniqlo.

**Uniqlo:** It's open-end and a bit rough, and I call it a starter t-shirt [2]. It has a bound neck collar that doesn't wiggle [3]. Earlier I said the heavyweight crew may be the best bargain t-shirt [4]. My shrink tests on the two Uniqlo tees were about 2.3 to 2.5% in width and 2% in length [5]. If you're taller or wider, I'd look at Muji instead [2].

**The Front General Store:** It's a $40 shirt made entirely in Japan, with great proportions and feel [6]. I think it's one of the best shirts you can get if you want an upgrade and don't want to spend over $40 [7]. When I picked a favorite in the best-value category, I went with Front General Store, though I might pick House of Blanks another day [8].

**Pro Club:** It's the roughest shirt in that comparison, but I like everything about it [9]. Its softness scored 4 out of 10, and it shrank 2.78% in width and 6.86% in length [10].

**Hanes:** It's a classic $10 shirt, and much softer than Pro Club [11]. It scored 7 out of 10 for softness, with shrinkage of 1.45% in width and 6.73% in length [12].

**My take:**
- **Best value:** Uniqlo.
- **Best upgrade:** Front General Store.
- **Cheapest options:** Hanes is softer and Pro Club is rougher, but both shrank noticeably more in length than Uniqlo in my tests.

questions.question: Would you recommend this [Barbour Bedale] or the flint and tinder for someone who would use it like a rain jacket but also a windbreaker and a spring light jacket?

hybrid.answer:
I'd lean toward the Barbour Bedale for what you describe, with caveats. I haven't said anything about the Flint and Tinder's rain or wind performance, so that comparison is incomplete.

**Barbour Bedale**
- It was the top pick of the waxed jackets I looked at, with 186 votes, well ahead of Flint and Tinder's 96 [1].
- It's the lightest-weight fabric of that group, and it has room to layer over, so it works in spring, fall or summer [2].
- For rain, a brand-new coat of wax didn't leak at all in my shower test [3]. How water-resistant it is depends on the state of the wax, and a worn jacket will let water in [4].
- It has storm cuffs [5] and a storm flap behind the zipper [6]. I'd also get the snap-on hood [7].
- For wind, I said the tighter weave of thornproof finishes adds wind and water resistance [8]. I haven't tested the Bedale specifically as a windbreaker.
- I'd treat any wax jacket as a rain jacket only with some caution, since waxed jackets in general aren't designated rain jackets [9].

**Flint and Tinder Waxed Trucker**
- I've said it's built for everyone. It isn't crazy lightweight but is lighter weight and comfortable [10]. That was in a sponsored segment, though I said I'd talked about the jacket many times before the sponsorship [11].
- It's lined, made in the US, and $300 [12].
- Earlier, I said it was for a specific man who isn't me, though I also said it wasn't a bad jacket [13]. In that video I described the canvas as exceedingly light [14].

**Bottom line:** Lightness suits your spring use, and both jackets are on the light side. For rain, I can point to the Bedale's tested water resistance and its rain features, plus the need to keep the wax up. I haven't covered how the Flint and Tinder handles rain or wind.

questions.question: Great video. But just curious, how can you say it's a con that the Huckberry jacket is unlined when they sell two different versions of lined waxed truckers: wool, and flannel?

hybrid.answer:
The con applies to the unlined Huckberry jacket I reviewed in that video. I know Huckberry also sells lined versions, and I like those more.

**Why I called it a con.** The jacket in that video is the cheapest, simplest, unlined one on the list [1]. I always like a lining on a waxed jacket so the wax isn't touching your clothes or arms, so for me, no lining is a drawback [2][3]. It's a personal preference. I also said that otherwise the jacket is flawless [3].

**The lined versions.** I've covered the lined one too. Huckberry also offers one without a lining, so the choice exists [4]. The lined Flint and Tinder is more comfortable because you don't get wax on your skin [5]. There is also a wool-lined version, which comes in much more limited quantity [6]. I haven't got that one yet, and I'd like to try it [5].

**Where I've softened.** I now see why you might leave a jacket unlined. Satin-lined sleeves can stick to your skin when it's a little warm, and that limits how often you can wear the jacket [7]. So I still prefer a lining, but I'm less hard on unlined jackets than I used to be.

questions.question: Do you know how these fit compared to the 875s? [Red Wing 3335s]

hybrid.answer:
I haven't directly compared the fit of the 3335s and the 875s in my videos, but I can tell you how the 3335s fit.

**3335 fit:** I went true to size and they fit fine. Sizing is pretty straightforward with Red Wings [1]. They have a slim, tapered profile because the outsole is very thin. With thin cotton socks I had no tightness, but with wool socks my toes feel squished and I can't wiggle them much [1].

**What I can say about the 875s:** I haven't described their fit. I did say the 875s and 1907s are more beefily constructed than the 3335s [2]. For the 1907 moc toe, I bought my usual boot size, an 8, and it fit perfectly. I also said leather Red Wings should be snug but not squished when new [3]. That is about the 1907, not the 875, so I wouldn't assume it carries over exactly.
